senate noun

classical

senātus, senātūs m.

noun, fourth declension

the senate

The council of the elders, named from senex, as Cicero says (Sen. 19). The Roman senate was a standing council of former magistrates, enrolled by the censors and sitting for life; it advised the magistrates, and its decrees (senātūs cōnsulta) were not laws. A modern senate is the upper house of a parliament and votes on laws; Latin keeps the word for it (Levi–Bini p. 46, of the Italian Senate). The senate house is cūria (Traupman 180).

Other words

  • camera superior — the upper house of a parliament

    noun phrase: camera with the adjective superior · also used · modern · M-O s.v. legislature: British: House of Lords

    Tursellinus’s name (1652) for the House of Lords; camera, classically a vaulted room (Lewis & Short), is Morgan–Owens’s word for a chamber of a parliament.

Examples

  • quae nisi essent in senibus, nōn summum cōnsilium majōrēs nostrī appellāssent senātum

    if these qualities were not found in old men, our ancestors would not have called their highest council the senateCic. Sen. 19

  • senātus fidem atque ingenium puerī exōsculātur

    the senate warmly praised the boy’s loyalty and witGell. 1.23.13
